newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish Islamist leader pins hopes on sell-offs.
newsitem.headline: Turkish Islamist leader pins hopes on sell-offs.

text.p: Turkish prime minister Necmettin Erbankan, aiming to meet ambitious budget goals, appears to have taken a radical turn towards massive and quick privatisations.

"Erbakan is seeking to accelerate privatisation next year. He wants to use proceeds of privatisation in productive fields, which will help Turkey attain high growth rate in coming years," said one of his close aides who declined to be named.
Already, a privatisation official said iron and steel company Eregli might be put on sale this week through newspaper adds in Turkey and abroad.
And the High Board of Privatisation, headed by Erbakan, met on Tuesday to study ongoing projects.

"Today, we discussed our determination for privatisation," Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller of the True Path Party told reporters after a meeting with Erbakan on Tuesday. "We will make decisive implementations on privatisation in coming days."
The True Path Party is Erbankan's coalition partner and a leading advocate of privatisation.
For about a decade before coming to power, Erbakan appeared as a firm opponent to selling state assets to foreigners, but now, he has pinned his hopes on a privatisation.
The radical change in Erbakan's approach towards privatisation is not ideological but neccessary.

Economists said his over-ambitious economic goals, which include a balanced budget, narrow trade and current account deficits and lower inflation, would only be achieved through a massive influx of foreign capital.
And privatisation is seen as the easiest way of securing foreign funds for Erbakan as Turkey's sub-investment credit rating restricts hard currency inflow through foreign borrowing.
Since 1986, Turkey has raised only $3 billion because of political turmoils, legal barriers, court annulments and lack of consensus on the benefits of privatisation.

But now, most of the barriers before sell-offs have been removed and political turmoil has faded since the establishment of Erbakan's Islamist-conservative coalition in late June. Many Turks, even some communists, are now reconciled to the idea of downsizing the unproductive state sector.
The World Bank, IMF and Turkish businessmen also support efforts to speed up privatisation.
As a result, Erbakan aims to complete sell-offs worth some $15 billion next year. He said $6.9 billion would come from privatisation of power plants through leasing.

But analysts cautioned that his efforts might fail due to lack of available domestic funds and low foreign interest in the companies on the sell-off programme, which would stymie efforts to generate expected proceeds from sell-offs next year.

"An annual privatisation revenue of $15 billion is a huge figure and unrealistic," said a government economist who asked not to be named. "Such a big amount can not be raised from cash-short domestic sources, and foreigners may not be willing to invest that amount in Turkish shares as many other coutries float their telecoms and other shares in international markets."
"Half of it, something around $7 billion, should be seen as a successful implementation," she said.

The centre of the government's privatisation programme is expected to be the sale of a minority stake in telecommunications giant Turk Telekom, which is seen bringing in some 3.5 billion next year and $1 billion by transferring GSM licenses to private companies.
But Erbakan's aide said the process to price Turk Telekom could easily be completed by February.
"The adviser to run Turk Telekom deal can be choosen this month. Bids have been collected from the short-listed consortia. This is not a new project. It started years ago," he said.

Though past attempts to sell Turk Telekom have been hindered by constitutional challenges, the aide said the government may raise funds through convertible bond issues for companies if privatisation faces an obstacle.

The Privatisation Administration (OIB) also plans to raise around $4 billion in 1997 by selling companies in its portfolio. Administration officials said major sell-off projects developed in the past five years could easily be completed in 1997.
Minority stakes in Tupras refineries, petroelum retailer Petrol Ofisi and Petkim petrochemicals firm and Eregli could be privately-held by 1997.
